keyTakeaways: AI can accelerate script preparation and translation drafting, but performance-ready surtitles still require source verification, human review, rehearsal, operation, and audience support.
A script import should produce an inspectable, editable cue draft rather than hide parsing uncertainty or claim perfect automation.
Projection, mobile viewing, spreadsheets, and PowerPoint exports can all be valid outputs; the team must keep one approved source of truth.
A professional live-text workflow is accountable, reviewable, rehearsed, and recoverable when performance departs from the expected path.

faq.question: Can AI turn a theatre script directly into finished surtitles?
faq.answer: No. AI and document analysis can help prepare an editable draft, but teams still need to verify script structure, shape readable cue units, review every language, rehearse timing, and test the audience delivery path.

faq.question: Why use a dedicated workflow instead of PowerPoint?
faq.answer: PowerPoint can be a practical display tool. A dedicated workflow adds value when a team needs one traceable source, editable cue and language decisions, rehearsal-linked revisions, multiple outputs, and clearer live recovery.

faq.question: How should AI translation be used for theatre surtitles?
faq.answer: Use it as an editor-time drafting stage after the source and cue structure are stable enough. A competent reviewer must compare source and target, edit for reading conditions, and approve the text before performance.

faq.question: What should be checked before theatre surtitles go live?
faq.answer: Check the source version, parsing, cue boundaries, language approval, audience instructions, representative seats and devices, operator rehearsal, ownership of every delivery path, and a tested fallback.

glossary.definition: An editable first structure of likely performance-text units that still requires human verification and shaping.
The single approved version from which live text and controlled exports are derived.
Automation whose inputs, outputs, uncertainty, and changes remain visible enough for a person to inspect and correct.
The operator's rehearsed ability to return audience text to the performance when lines are skipped, repeated, reordered, or cut.
A defined check of content, audience experience, operation, ownership, and fallback before opening the service to an audience.
